title: Lost cylinders of Buddy Bolden and Emmett Hardy
summary: Allen and Wiggs discuss unfound cylinders of Bolden and Hardy and the conflicting accounts of Hardy's style.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Oh, yes. But, of course, some of them have never been found. There are some cylinders, like of a legendary figure, Buddy Bolden. We know about him from the people who played with him, the people who heard him, but no one's ever found this cylinder. Emmett Hardy, too, from New Orleans. Buddy Bolden was from New Orleans, too. Yes. Emmett Hardy was one of the people that they named as a possible influence on Big Spiderbeck, who Johnny mentioned before. I believe there must be something to that, because I've talked to Mark Hazel about it, and I've talked to people like Johnny Barstorfer, who's now dead. Both of those men are now dead. And they said that this was confirmed by Biggs and by Emmett Hardy. But who knows? We have no records of Emmett Hardy. We only can go by the words of the men who knew them and heard them.
It's supposed to be a cylinder, you know, just like a Buddy Bolden.
Yes. Of Emmett Hardy's. They've hunted and hunted for that. And it's supposed to have been done on an old Addison dictaphone machine.

Of course, I was in New York. I had to be in New York when Emmett Hardy was playing. And ever since I've heard about Emmett Hardy, I've just been crazy to try to get somebody, a Harry Shields and Raymond Blake and all of them.
Played with him to try to give me the lowdown on him at Hardy's playing. And to this day, I have never gotten a tale that would match up with the other one. So I still don't
